text.0_, 86_Siman, 2_Seif, 0_Paragraph: "But meat of a pure animal in milk that is impure etc." The Tur says, 'but pure meat (of a kosher animal) in impure milk (milk from a non-kosher animal) or impure meat in pure milk, and meat of a chicken and non-domesticated kosher animal in pure milk is only a rabbinic prohibition for eating and are permitted to cook and receive benefit.' And the Beit Yosef writes, '[the Tur] did not intend to write this language since we don't see this language, that it is only rabbinic, for the first two cases, but only for the non-domesticated animal and chicken in pure milk. This is because in the case of pure meat in impure milk or the opposite, the Rabbis did not prohibit to eat because of mixing meat and milk. They did not establish any Rabbinic prohibitions [in this case], since it is already a Torah prohibition to consume impure meat or impure milk.' This is the corrected way to understand the text [of the Tur] and it is the proper understanding. However, the Bach understands the Tur as is written, that the first two cases are rabbinic prohibitions of mixing meat and milk. The practical reason being 'the piece becomes carrion'/ChaNaN (חנ"נ\ חתיכה נעשית נבילה explained in siman 92) which only applies in the case of mixing meat and milk and also to the case of 'the piece that is proper for serving' look there. This is the opinion of the Perisha. According to this, which is how we hold, ChaNaN applies to all forbidden foods, as the [Rema] writes in siman 92 seif 4 see there and search. This is also clear from Rashi and the Ran (Chapter All the Meat - Chullin 113a in the mishna) that [ChaNaN] is not a prohibition based on mixing meat and milk at all even rabbinically, and there is no reason at all that the Rabbis would prohibit on the basis of mixing meat and milk. It makes sense that the Rabbis prohibited mixing chicken with milk, lest one think they can also eat other meat milk, as the Rambam states there. However, the notion to prohibit pure meat with impure milk or vice versa has no reason to worry  about transgressing another prohibited act. This seems to be the intention of the Beit Yosef in not prohibiting [pure meat and impure milk or vice versa] on the basis of mixing meat and milk, unlike the Bach, since it is already forbidden by the Torah and there is no reason to make a decree [fence to protect against another act]. The Beit Yosef is saying that there is no practical case to prohibit on the basis of mixing meat and milk. And this is also the ruling for the case of 'the piece that is proper for serving' which explained later in seif 110. Also the Drisha writes at the end there that there is no place that pure meat and impure milk or vice versa has a rabbinic prohibition and is considered carrion on a rabbinic basis.

text.0_, 86_Siman, 6_Seif, 0_Paragraph: According to the opinion of the Rav where he says that "all the more so [is it forbidden ab initio to cook meat in impure milk]," we need to resolve that which is written in the Tur Seif 3 that [meat and impure milk] are permitted to cook together and to derive benefit from. This is based on a literal Mishnah in chapter Kol Habasar [chapter 8 of Hullin]. And this is agreed upon by all the Poskim, meaning that it is permitted in practice according to Halacha. However, due to the concern for mar'it ha'ayin (appearance of impropriety), it is not advisable to do so. A practical implication would be situations where there is no concern for the appearance of impropriety, such as in the case of medical treatment and the like. Like that which the Maharshal wrote in 25:102, that [cooking] breastmilk [with meat] for health reasons is permitted, "even if there is no danger at all, since there is no prohibition involved except for mar'it ha'ayin." There are also other situations where there is no concern of mar'it ha'ayin. And this resolves what was left unanswered in the Torat Hatat regarding the Rashba. Indeed the words of the poskim who wrote generally that [milk from a non-kosher animal] is permissible to cook imply that even regarding mar'it ha'ayin, there is no concern. And such is found in the writing of the Maharshal, Perek 25. And this is the implied opinion of the Mechaber, who did not write that the milk of an impure animal is forbidden because of mar'it ha'ayin. Therefore, it seems clear to me that there, it is different since in any case, one of them (i.e., either the milk or the meat) is prohibited to eat, since there is definitely no issue with cooking per se, because you could have been cooking for medicinal or other purposes. When we say it is forbidden to cook them, we mean to eat them. What the mehaber says in seif 5 "it is forbidden to cook them," that must also mean to eat them. We see often in Scripture and Mishnah that eating is referred to as cooking. It's only in these cases [of eating] that there is mar'it ha'ayin.

Even though it is embedded in sinews, etc., and that which appears earlier in section 86 paragraph 4, regarding one who struck a hen on its tail and it laid eggs, that they are forbidden due to the prohibition of a limb from a living creature if they are embedded in sinews—even if the yolk and white are fully formed—this implies that since they are embedded, they are considered like the flesh of the hen. However, this case is different, because regarding the prohibition of meat with milk from fowl, which is rabbinic, they were lenient; alternatively, this case is different because each component is permitted on its own. So wrote the later authorities, and this distinction is mentioned in Tosafot and the halakhic decisors, including the Rashba, who distinguish between the case of an egg from a carcass earlier in section 86 paragraph 3, which is forbidden, and this case here. And it seems to me that even without this, there is no difficulty from the case of the hen struck on its tail, for even though it is not considered flesh, nevertheless, even actual milk would be forbidden due to the prohibition of a limb from a living creature, were it not for the verse that revealed to us “a land flowing with milk and honey,” as mentioned above in section 81 subparagraph 11. If so, the verse that permits milk does so because it is not connected to anything and does not separate from flesh, but eggs that are embedded and attached are certainly in their state of prohibition. And even more than this, there are those who forbid even milk fluids due to the prohibition of a limb from a living creature, as mentioned above in section 81. And although we do not rule according to them, the reasons explained there are still significant. In any case, certainly embedded eggs are forbidden to all opinions due to the prohibition of a limb from a living creature. Furthermore, Rabbeinu Tam wrote that even fully formed eggs would be forbidden due to this prohibition were it not for the verse that permits them, as written in the Sha’arim section 64 and other decisors in his name. Therefore, certainly when they are embedded, and no verse permits them, they are forbidden due to the prohibition of a limb from a living creature, and this is clear.
text.0_, 86_Siman, 9_Seif, 0_Paragraph: But if it contains only the yolk, etc.,it implies that even if it is not embedded, anything that has not developed beyond the yolk is considered like the flesh of the bird, as the Rashba wrote. In my writings I elaborated on this and concluded that ideally one should not eat with milk even those eggs that have developed both yolk and white but still have a soft shell, even if they are not embedded—according to the views of the Rashbam, Mordechai, Agudah (first chapter of Beitzah), Sha’arim section 76, Or Zarua, and Mahari in his glosses to Sefer HaDinim. However, after the fact, if they were cooked with milk, it seems they are permitted. But if they are embedded, even after the fact they are forbidden, since the Bahag (page 35b) ruled like Rabbi Yaakov, and this is the version found in all manuscripts of the Rif in the first chapter of Beitzah. It is also written in Shiltei Giborim (chapter 25, page 315a) in the name of the Rif, and the opinion of the Ran also supports this unless one emends his words in chapter 25. This is also the view of Rabbi Yonatan as cited in Orach Chaim and Kol Bo section 105, and it is evident that the Rashbam and his supporters hold that the halacha follows Rabbi Yaakov, for otherwise the sugya in the first chapter of Beitzah cannot be reconciled according to their view. So too wrote the Agudah explicitly in section 62, and the Jerusalem Talmud also rules clearly like Rabbi Yaakov. This is also implied somewhat in our Babylonian Talmud, which, after two versions, concludes by establishing the baraita according to him and not like the Geonim who left the Rif’s ruling as a difficulty. Also, the Beit Yosef and other later authorities wrote simply that all the poskim ruled like the first tanna, but this is incorrect, as I have already proven. The main definition of “developed” refers to eggs that have developed both yolk and white. If those with soft shells are embedded, they are forbidden even after the fact; if not embedded, they are permitted. But those small eggs that have developed only the yolk, even if not embedded, are forbidden even after the fact, for they are like the flesh of the bird. So ruled the Tashbetz in section 70, although he did not distinguish between embedded or not, and it seems from his words that those which have developed both yolk and white are permitted after the fact even if embedded. The main ruling is as I have written. It is also somewhat puzzling why no emendation was made here. Nevertheless, it seems that even if only the yolk has developed and they are embedded, one may be lenient in cases of significant loss, and in such cases it is fitting to rely on Rashi, Tosafot, the Rosh, the Tur, and Rabbi Yerucham. It also seems that according to their view, “embedded” refers to those small eggs that have developed only the yolk and are attached to the spinal flesh, and not as the Beit Yosef wrote that according to the Tur quoting Rashi, it refers to when they have separated from the spinal flesh and contain red streaks. The Ateret Zekenim followed this interpretation, but Rashi himself did not explain it that way. Also, in both the first and second versions in the Talmud, it is clearly proven not like the Beit Yosef but as I have explained. Furthermore, the words of the Maharshal in chapter 25 section 12 are puzzling on this matter and contradict each other compared to what he wrote in chapter 1 of Beitzah section 19—see there. All this is from a legal standpoint. However, Mahari wrote—and it seems that women do not follow the leniency even when the eggs are fully developed and the outer shell is completely hard—see there. The Maharshal and the author of Tashbetz followed this custom. Nevertheless, it seems from the words of Mahari and the others that this is merely a stringency, and therefore in places where there is no established custom, one need not be concerned about it at all. The Bach tried to find a reason to say that the custom is law, but his words are not compelling—see there.

text.0_, 86_Siman, 15_Seif, 0_Paragraph: “And male milk is not called milk, etc.” — this implies that since it is not classified as “milk,” and there is not even a rabbinic prohibition, it does not render the food forbidden. However, in the Or Zarua HaGadol (Orah Hayim) it is written that it is no worse than a woman’s milk. From the words of the Maggid Mishneh (chapter 9 of Hilchot Ma’achalot Asurot), it appears that male milk is rabbinically prohibited, and he writes that this also seems to be the view of the Rambam, whose language the Shulchan Aruch adopts. This is also somewhat implied in the Talmud (Beitzah 25b), where Shmuel says: “There, [the verse refers to] the milk of its mother, not the milk of a male; the milk of its mother, not the milk of a slaughtered animal.” If so, since both are excluded from a single verse, and we hold that the milk of a slaughtered animal is at least rabbinically forbidden (as will be explained below in section 90), so too male milk. It seems that the Maggid Mishneh is referring to male milk from an animal, as Rashi explains in the Talmud there: “Not the milk of a male, who had a small amount of milk from the teats, such as if they changed and developed teats.” This is also how the Maharshal explains it in section 100. And this is clearly implied in the Talmud, which later asks: “What is the law regarding one who cooks in the milk of a kid that never nursed?” He replied: “Since Shmuel needed to say ‘the milk of its mother, not the milk of a male,’ it is because a male cannot become a mother. But this one, since it could become a mother, it is forbidden.” This proves that the discussion is about male milk from an animal. But male human milk is certainly no worse than a woman’s milk. According to this, the Shulchan Aruch, which quotes the Rambam’s language—implying that male milk is exempt from lashes but still forbidden—and the gloss of the Rema do not disagree.

text.0_, 92_Siman, 0_Seif, 0_Paragraph:
It is forbidden when one gives to taste:
Meaning, he should let a cook taste whether there is in it taste, as we established earlier in the beginning of siman 92 and 98, and such is written in the Beis Yosef. And the Rama goes according to his own reasoning, in that he writes in those places that we are not accustomed to rely on the tasting of a non-jew. Therefore he writes "And one needs to measure against the whole pot".
And although it is implied in many places that that there is not in the volume of the amount contained in the utensil (the pot) sixty times the whole utensil (the walls and floor of the pot), one might answer that nevertheless, he is saying that one needs to measure it against the whole pot, and that therefore it will (always) be forbidden.

Alternatively, we find sometimes that the width of the pot is so big that it holds an amount of water that will be sixty times it (the walls and floor of the pot). For example if the copper (the material the pot is made of) is thin, but very wide, and like the Beis Yosef writes.

But in any case, this that we would need to measure (the contents of the pot) against the whole (walls and floor of the) pot, is by a used pot, that we don't know how much it has absorbed. But if we know how much it has absorbed, one need only measure against that amount that it had absorbed, as is said in 92:5 in the Rama, and in 94:6 and many places. And the same goes for when it was used, and we don't know how much was absorbed, but we know how much was cooked in it within 24 hours from the cooking of this milk, since what was cooked in it before 24 hours is nosein ta'am lifgam. And even if some meat was cooked in it within 24 hours of cooking the first meat, one does not need sixty times anything other than the second meat, and consider this.
text.0_, 92_Siman, 1_Seif, 0_Paragraph: AGAINST THE WHOLE POT: And later in Siman 98 he will explain that there is no difference between a pot of metal or of earthenware, one always needs to measure it against the whole pot, see there.
text.0_, 92_Siman, 2_Seif, 0_Paragraph:
BUT THE POT IS FORBIDDEN TO COOK IN IT, NOT MEAT AND NOT MILK: Since it has absorbed both of them. Therefore, it is forbidden to cook meat in it from the outset (lechatchila) even after 24 hours from cooking now, the same way it is forbidden to cook milk from the outset in a pot of meat after 24 hours. However if he cooked meat in it WITHIN 24 hours of cooking milk in it, it's obvious that the food will be forbidden (even after the fact). But if he cooked milk it's obvious that it will be permitted after the fact.

However, other things that aren't of meat or of milk (pareve items), such as vegetables and fish and things like that, are permitted to cook in it even from the outset.

And later in 94:5 the Rama writes that the custom is to forbid a utensil that had been left for 24 hours even for other things (pareve), even when one had only dipped a spoon that had been used within 24 hours. If so, certainly (the custom applies) here where one cooked actual meat in it. We must explain that here he minced words regarding the halacha. And see what I wrote there in siman 94.

AND IT IS A STRINGENCY WITHOUT ANY REASON

Nevertheless, in Toras Chatos 85:4 he writes a bit of a reason according the ones stringent, which is that they hold that the prohibitions of steam (see 92:8) and smell (see 108) are stronger than that which is on account of taste itself. And he writes (quote) that it is only with those covers that are short (confined) on top, and which have in them something like a cavity as there is in many covers, and are therefore impossible to to clean well enough to be pure of any steaming or simmering that ascended there. But those that are wide (easily accessible) on top, and one's hand is able to reach in them to scrub them well, we do not say that there is physical issur (leftover), and it is permitted, end quote.

And according to his words we are forced to say that even though that which is in the confined space is a small amount (which should generally be batul beshishim), nevertheless the steam of the meat rises above (into that confined space) less than 60 times it, until it makes the physical amount (in the confined space) neveila, and subsequently the cover itself becomes neveila, as in 98:5, that there may not be 3660 times, minus a bit, the physical amount (in the confined space), and it is similar to what we said earlier in 92:5, see there.

But at any rate one definitely need not be so stringent when dealing with a cover, just as the Rama says here. And this is what is said in Aphei Ravrevei 61a, that in extenuating circumstances, or if there is any other reason to permit it, or if it is a wide cover, or if it is perforated on top, it would seem that one may permit it. And in addition, the Darchei Moshe screams bloody murder about this minhag, since it is a mistaken minhag, and it has no reason to explain it. And even the Ateres Zahav calls foul on this minhag.

text.0_, 101_Siman, 7_Seif, 0_Paragraph:
[Regarding the law of] a vessel, etc., because it is necessary, etc.The Maharshal wrote (Chapter 25, end of section 86) that there was no need for this reason of spending one's money [to kasher the vessel]. This is because even without this reason, since the permitting state (היתר) does not arrive automatically by the mere passage of time, it is not considered a Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin (an item that will eventually become permitted). Thus far are his words.

The Shakh's Counter-Argument:

However, I do not comprehend his reasoning (ולא ירדתי לסוף דעתו). For behold, even if the permitting state arrives without the passage of time, it is still considered a Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin—such as in the case of vows (נדרים) and the like [where absolution can be requested at any time].

Alternative Views on Mixed Vessels:

The Ra'ah in Bedek HaBayit (page 128b) objects to the Rashba, arguing that there is a completely different reason here why the vessel cannot be nullified, independent of the laws of Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin. His reasoning is that wherever a prohibition is recognizable, it cannot be nullified; and since it is possible to extract the absorbed prohibition from within the vessel via Hag'alah (purification in boiling water), it is viewed as if the prohibition is actively recognizable. Furthermore, it is impossible for these vessels not to impart a forbidden taste into the permitted food. See there where he elaborates.

The Maharil in his Responsa (Section 194) also disagrees with the Rashba. He argues that the financial expense required to perform Hag'alah is considered a minor loss (הפסד מועט). This is comparable to what we calculate in the Talmudic chapter HaZahav (Bava Metzia 53) and in the seventh chapter of Nedarim, where Second Tithe (מעשר שני) is considered to have a permitting mechanism because it can be brought up to Jerusalem [despite the travel expense]. See there. Therefore, one should take his words into account in any situation where there is no substantial financial loss (הפסד מרובה).

Waiting 24 Hours (Eino Ben Yomo):

It also appears to me that one should leave the mixed vessels until they are no longer "of their day" (Eino Ben Yomo, meaning 24 hours have passed), for at that point, the absorbed taste becomes foul and is permitted by Torah law. The author of the Responsa Mas'at Binyamin wrote similarly at the end of his work. However, he noted there that this requirement to wait applies specifically if one intends to use the vessels all together as a group; but to use a single vessel on its own is permitted immediately, because since there is nothing present but absorbed taste, it does not fall under the strictures of Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin.

In my humble opinion, however, even using each vessel individually is forbidden until a full 24-hour cycle (מעת לעת) has passed. For the Rashba and the Tur only ruled that a vessel is not treated as a Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin because one must incur financial expenses to permit it; but in a case like this, where a permitting mechanism naturally occurs by Torah law without any financial expense [simply by waiting 24 hours], everyone agrees it is forbidden to use immediately. Furthermore, later in subparagraph 9, I have established the halakhic conclusion that even a forbidden taste (טעמא) is not nullified when dealing with a Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin.

Refuting a Stringency from the Bach:

In the Responsa of Ibn Lev, he ruled that if a dairy bowl becomes mixed among meat bowls, it cannot be nullified by a majority because it is a mixture Shelo Be'mino (not of its own kind), and therefore all the bowls become forbidden. The Bach has already taken issue with this ruling.

Additionally, the Bach was stringent to require removing one vessel from the mixture as a mere stringency, comparing it to the custom of the Maharam who would discard one piece of meat from a mixture. However, this comparison is incorrect. All the Halakhic authorities agree later in Section 109 that it is completely unnecessary to remove a piece. As for the Maharam who did so, the Mahara"i explained the reason: the Maharam was an extraordinarily righteous man and a preeminent Torah scholar who took a personal stringency upon himself because it felt disgraceful to him that the consumption of a prohibition should happen to come to his mouth. This reasoning does not apply to vessels.

Nevertheless, in a situation where no financial loss is involved, it is proper to be stringent in accordance with the words of the Bach. Analyze this closely.
text.0_, 101_Siman, 8_Seif, 0_Paragraph:
Regarding the rule that an item that will eventually become permitted (Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin) is not nullified... but its taste is nullified. And regarding the ruling (in the first section) that if they whitened/glazed food with it or stuffed a chicken with it, it is not nullified—this is because it is considered the actual physical substance of the prohibition. It is not considered dissolved and lacking visible presence, except when it is entirely unrecognizable in appearance and exists only as a taste. Thus far are the words of the Torat Chatat there (Section 2) in the name of the Mahara"i.

The Shakh's Challenge:

However, this requires further study. For in my humble opinion, it appears from the Talmud in Nedarim (98) and the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 6 of Nedarim), as well as Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Ran there in Nedarim, that regarding a Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin, even its taste is not nullified when mixed with its own kind (min be'mino). See there.
This is also proven from what the Maharam and the Rosh wrote in a responsum (Beginning of Principle 2) regarding beer made from new grain (Chadash), stating that the grain is nullified in sixty parts water, and when we say a Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin is not nullified, that specifically applies when it is mixed with its own kind. This is also implied by the Rambam, the Smag, and the Author [Shulchan Arukh] later in section 216:10 regarding forbidden wine that became mixed into other wine: even a single drop in a barrel forbids the whole mixture, because he can request absolution for his vow.

Refuting the Torat Chatat's Sources:

Also, what the Torat Chatat wrote there—that this is the opinion of the Tur, Orach Chayim 513 in the name of Rabbeinu Tam—is not a compelling proof. In my humble opinion, the Tur only stated there that in a mixture not of its own kind (shelo be'mino), we do not apply the rule that a Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin cannot be nullified, as is proven in the Beit Yosef and the Bach there, see there and analyze closely. This is precisely what the Tur wrote here in the name of Rabbeinu Tam: "The rule that a Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin is not nullified applies specifically when it is mixed with its own kind, but when not mixed with its own kind, its taste is nullified in sixty." Consequently, in its own kind, even its taste is not nullified.

Furthermore, what the Rav [Rema] wrote in the Torat Chatat—that this is the opinion of the Issur V'Heter (Principle 25)—is incorrect. For he ruled there in Law 4 just like the Rambam regarding the wine mentioned above, and similarly regarding vessels that absorbed a prohibition, he wrote there in Law 19 like the Rashba and the Author in section 3. And regarding what he wrote there in Law 17—that an item whose forbidden substance is not visibly present and only its taste remains is nullified—that refers specifically to a mixture not of its own kind.

Here is his exact quote there: "The rule that a Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin is not nullified applies specifically in its own kind, but in not its own kind it is properly nullified in sixty, even if he does not recognize it and the body of the prohibition remains inside it... And all the more so an item whose forbidden substance is not visibly present and there is nothing but mere taste, which is properly nullified in sixty. And so we learned in the Jerusalem Talmud that for a Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin, the Sages did not assign a standard measure, but rather in its own kind [it forbids] in any amount, and in not its own kind [it forbids] by imparting taste." Behold, it is explicit that he is dealing specifically with a mixture not of its own kind.

A Proposed Resolution and its Rejection:

Seemingly, one could have somewhat resolved his [the Rema's] words in the gloss by saying: Wherever the actual body of the prohibition is still in the mixture, even though it is not visibly present—like wine in wine and similar cases—it is not nullified. But where a piece of forbidden food fell in and he subsequently threw it out whole—where we maintain that even so, one must nullify the exudate (as stated earlier in section 98:8) because of the taste that came out of it—in such a case it is nullified. From this, we could resolve some of the earlier proofs, as they deal with situations where the body of the item itself was mixed in, which is why it is not nullified.

However, from his words in the Torat Chatat there, it appears he makes no such distinction. He derived this from Orach Chayim section 513, which explicitly deals with the body of the item being mixed in, see there. This is also proven from the words of the Mahara"i that he brought there, which I cited at the beginning of this subparagraph, analyze closely. Furthermore, he derived this law from the Hagahot Asheri (Chapter 2 of Avodah Zarah) in the name of the Mahari"ch, and there it says explicitly: "Specifically where there is substance to the prohibition, but if there is no substance to the prohibition and it dissolved, it is nullified in sixty." This is also implied in the Darkhei Moshe.

Final Ruling:

But in truth, regarding the final Halakhah, it appears that even if he removed the forbidden piece whole, its taste is not nullified, as is seemingly implied by all the aforementioned proofs. This is also proven from what Rabbeinu Yeruham wrote (Path 14, Part 4): "One who vowed [not to benefit] from meat, and eggs were cooked with the meat—they are forbidden by imparting taste, for even though it is a Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin, [it is nullified only] because it is not its own kind."

Regardless, it is a strained logic to differentiate between whether its taste remains there along with its physical substance or not. For ultimately, the logic stands: "Until you eat it in prohibition, eat it in permissibility."

Later, I found in the Bach that he also ruled there is no distinction, and it is never nullified, though he abbreviated the matter, see there. And see the following subparagraph.

The Laws of Safek‑Safeka (Double Doubt).
1) This is not considered a safek‑safeka. Even if the first doubt was not known until after the mixture occurred — for example, several eggs were mixed together, and afterward a doubt of terefah was discovered in a chicken, and it became known that one of the eggs came from that chicken and was laid after the doubt of terefah arose — and similarly in all such cases: Even though no doubt of prohibition was known at all until after the mixture, and therefore both doubts became known together and arrived simultaneously, nevertheless, since the first doubt involves a biblical prohibition, it is not considered a safek‑safeka. So ruled the Darkei Moshe, end of siman 57, and the Taz, Klal 43, din 7. But the Avi Ezri, at the end of siman 57, quoting the Mahari”k, disagreed and permitted the case even when the first doubt was not known before the mixture, because of safek‑safeka.And this is what the Rema concludes in his gloss: “But if there are two doubts whether any prohibition exists at all, and both doubts became known together…” — implying that in the first case, even when both doubts became known together, it is not a safek‑safeka.
And this also appears from the words of the poskim, and not like the responsum of Mish’at Binyamin, siman 37, who challenged the Rema on this point. His main argument was that from the source where the Rema derived this ruling — the Or Zarua HaGadol, Klal 26 — it does not appear this way. Rather, he claimed that only in the glosses on the Or Zarua is this written, and that we should rely more on the author of the Or Zarua himself, who was a great and authoritative rabbi, than on the glosses.
But this is not correct.
For in the Or Zarua itself it is clear in many places that even when the doubt was not known beforehand, it is still forbidden.
He writes in his conclusion that the two doubts are not from the same category:
The first doubt is inherent — “perhaps it is not a terefah.”
Only after the mixture does the second doubt arise — “perhaps this is not the forbidden one.”
Furthermore, the two doubts are not in the same object: If you say it is a terefah, perhaps this is not the egg — meaning two separate bodies.
But when the two doubts are in the same body — for example, in the case of safek tachtav (“doubt whether the blood came from under her”) or the case of a man and woman who relieved themselves into the same vessel (Niddah 59b, explained later in siman 191:6) — then the blood itself contains a safek‑safeka:
“Perhaps it is not from the woman,”
and if it is from the woman, “perhaps it came from the vestibule.”Thus, according to both reasons, even if the doubt was not known beforehand, the two doubts are not from the same category nor from the same body.
And furthermore, he writes that this case is not comparable to safek tachtav or the case of the man and woman — and in those cases, certainly the doubt was not known beforehand.
And this is evident to anyone who examines the Or Zarua in many places: he does not distinguish between whether the doubt was known beforehand or not. And the glosses on the Or Zarua are merely explanations of his words. This is clear.

and if it is a terefah, ‘perhaps at the time it became a terefah the egg already had its shell.’ For regarding the egg itself, the two doubts involve two different bodies, and the doubts are not from the same category, and the chicken had a presumption of being a terefah at the time it laid the egg or at the time the egg was found inside it.

4) And this is specifically when the egg is definitely from a chicken that had a doubt of terefah (as above), or when there is a doubt whether it is from a definitely terefah chicken (and there is also a doubt whether it had its shell before the chicken became terefah or not)―for example, an egg found in a courtyard where there are only two chickens, one kosher and one terefah. But if the chicken itself only has a doubt of terefah, then the egg is permitted even without any mixture at all, because of a safek‑safeka:
- perhaps the chicken did not lay this egg, and even if it did lay it,
- perhaps it is not a terefah.
And even though the mixture is only “one against one” (meaning: the chickens themselves were mixed one with one; but if the chickens had not first been mixed one with one, and each was still identifiable, then the first doubt would be a biblical doubt—because how could you later say “and if it is from this one, perhaps it is not a terefah,” when you have already forbidden it from the Torah because of the doubt—consider this well), nevertheless the first doubt is not considered a biblical safek de‑oraita, as will be explained below, since the chicken is not definitely terefah. And the two doubts are in one matter and one body, and they arise simultaneously. So ends his words.
And it seems that in this last ruling, it is permitted even when it is known that at the time the doubt of terefah arose in the chicken, the egg had not yet formed its shell—because of this safek‑safeka:
* perhaps the chicken did not lay it and the egg is not from it,
* and even if it is from it, perhaps the chicken is not a terefah.
And this is not comparable to the case of a doubtful egg of a terefah that became mixed, where all are forbidden and we do not permit through safek‑safeka, because there the doubts are not from one matter and one body.
For in that case, you cannot begin by saying “perhaps there is no prohibition here at all,” since there is certainly a doubtful terefah in this mixture. You are therefore forced to begin by saying “perhaps it is not a terefah,” and thus your first doubt is a biblical prohibition.
And when you then say, “and if it is a terefah, perhaps this is not the one,” in the second doubt you are being lenient and saying “perhaps this is not it,” which makes it two bodies and two separate matters.
This is unlike our case, where the starting point is that we do not know where this egg came from. Therefore you begin by saying, “perhaps it is from the kosher chicken, and there is no prohibition here at all.”
And when you later wish to be stringent and say, “perhaps it is from the terefah chicken,” then regarding this very body about which you wish to be stringent, I say: “perhaps it is not a terefah.”
And you cannot say: “But we already forbade it because of the doubt, and the first doubt is biblical,” because here the chickens were mixed one with one, and the first doubt is not biblical.
Therefore, even though the doubts are, in form, from two matters and two bodies, they are in truth from one body and one matter, since the first doubt is: “perhaps this egg is from the kosher chicken, and there is no prohibition here at all.”
Only when you come to be stringent and say, “perhaps it is from the terefah chicken,” and you thereby create two bodies and two matters in order to be stringent, I say: “perhaps it is not a terefah” in that very body and matter about which you are coming to be stringent.
And this is exactly comparable to the case of:
* “perhaps the blood is not from the woman, and if it is from the woman, perhaps it is from the vestibule.”
For even though there too the doubts are two matters and two bodies, they are truly from one matter and one body, as the Or Zarua wrote and I cited above in law (1).
The reason is that you certainly do not begin by saying “perhaps it is from the womb,” since at the outset we do not know where the blood came from at all.
Therefore, the first doubt is: from where did this blood come? And so at the beginning I say: “perhaps it is from the man, and there is no prohibition here at all,” and the first doubt is not a biblical prohibition.
And when you come to be stringent and judge with two bodies and two matters, saying that it is from the woman, I say to you regarding that very body you are judging—namely, the woman—“perhaps it is from the vestibule.”
And I found written in the handwriting of Rabbi Moshe Isserles in the margin of the Or Zarua on that case of an egg found in a courtyard, and it is not known whether it is from the kosher chicken or from the doubtful‑terefah chicken. His words:

“Nevertheless, the first doubt is not a biblical doubt, because the first doubt did not arise immediately, but only together with the second; whereas if the prohibition were based on a single doubt alone, then it would be called a biblical doubt of prohibition, as he wrote at the beginning of this responsum.”

End of his words—whose explanation is as I have written.
Therefore, it is also not considered a safek‑safeka in the case of a chicken in which a doubt of terefah arose recently, and it then laid an egg, and it is not known whether the egg was completed before that or not.
For when you begin by saying “doubt whether the chicken is terefah, doubt whether it is not terefah,” you are beginning with a doubt that is a biblical prohibition.
And when I say, “and if it is terefah,” you have still not yet created two bodies and two matters.
And when you then say, “perhaps the egg was completed earlier,” you are inventing another doubt to be lenient, with two bodies and two matters.
Similarly, even if you begin by saying, “and if it was not completed earlier, perhaps the chicken is not a terefah,” you are again being lenient with two bodies and two matters:
- at first you judged the egg itself,
- and now you come to judge and be lenient regarding the chicken—these are two bodies;
and at first you judged “perhaps it was completed earlier”, and now you come to judge and be lenient “perhaps it is not a terefah”—these are two matters.
Likewise, in a case where a single egg is found and it is not known whether it is from a definitely terefah chicken or from a kosher one—even though the chickens were mixed one with one—the first doubt is a biblical prohibition, since there is a definite prohibition in the chicken.
Therefore, you cannot say “perhaps it is from the kosher one,” because that would make the first doubt a biblical prohibition. And if you wish to begin by saying “perhaps the egg was completed earlier,” then all the more so you are beginning with a first doubt that is a biblical prohibition. And even when you then say, “and if it was completed later, perhaps it is not from the terefah but from the kosher one,” you are being lenient with two bodies and two matters. And furthermore, you have already said “perhaps it was completed later,” and thus you have admitted that it came from the terefah—so how can you then go back and say “it is not from it”?
And now it is also understood why, in the case of a doubtful terefah that became mixed into a thousand, all are forbidden—even to eat them one by one—while the second mixture is permitted even all at once, as explained above in se’if‑katan 55.
For what difference is there whether the first mixture is eaten two by two, or the second mixture is eaten all at once? In both cases there is a safek‑safeka.Furthermore, the second mixture is certainly permitted when it is not eaten all at once, because we can say: “perhaps this one that I am eating is not the one that fell here”—there you begin with two bodies. Rather, it must be that in the first mixture you cannot say “perhaps there is no prohibition here at all,” since there is certainly a doubtful terefah present. And you cannot begin by saying “perhaps this is not it,” because at the outset you must say: what is the defect in this very piece you are judging? And furthermore, if you begin by saying “perhaps this is not it,” then all the more so you are beginning with two bodies. Therefore, you are forced to begin with “perhaps it is not a terefah,” and thus your first doubt is a biblical prohibition. And even when you then say, “and if it is a terefah, perhaps this is not it,” you are being lenient with two bodies and two matters. But in the second mixture, I begin by saying: “perhaps there is no prohibition at all in this mixture,” and thus the first doubt is a doubt of something permitted by Torah law.
And when you wish to be stringent and say, “perhaps the prohibition that was in the first mixture fell into this one,” and you thereby create two bodies and two matters in order to be stringent, I say regarding this very body and matter about which you are saying that it is here: “perhaps it is not a terefah".

Even so, it does not help at all since the prohibition was established, for a living animal stands in a presumption of prohibition, and therefore any doubt in slaughter is not considered a doubt of prohibition but a certainty of prohibition due to the presumption. Also, the point that perhaps he did not slaughter the signs against the nick is not a doubt at all, for presumably he slaughtered in the manner of slaughterers and moved the knife back and forth across the entire blade. Furthermore, the Tosafot at the beginning of Chullin only wrote that this is “like” a double doubt. text.0_, 109_Siman, 63_Seif, 3_Paragraph: 29) It appears that even the Rav [the Rema] here in his gloss did not mean that we permit a Double Doubt in the face of a Presumption of Prohibition, except specifically in a case such as a broken wing of a bird, where the doubt does not concern the slaughter (shechitah) itself. This is also written in Darkei Moshe at the end of Chapter 57: "The Issur V'Heter wrote: even though we do not apply a Double Doubt to something that has a Presumption of Prohibition, nevertheless, where there is a remedy through inspection, it is permitted. For example, if a bird's wing was broken and we do not know if it happened before or after slaughter—and if you say it was before slaughter, perhaps the lung was not pierced—it is permitted based on a Double Doubt. Since there is a remedy through inspection to see if the lung was pierced, but we are simply stringent and do not inspect, the existence of a Double Doubt makes it permitted." Thus, it is explicit that the Rav's version of the Issur V'Heter HaAroch considered a broken wing to be a Presumption of Prohibition. Although our current editions of Issur V'Heter do not imply this (as will be explained), the Rav already wrote in Responsum 131, Law 12, that when he was writing and collecting his insights from the Issur V'Heter, he had a manuscript version where the language was styled differently, and many things there do not match the current printed editions. This resolves the Rav's challenge in Darkei Moshe and Torat Chatat against the Issur V'Heter's prohibition of a Double Doubt in a case of Presumption of Prohibition. He challenged this from the fact that the Tur (Chapter 57) and other authorities seek to permit a doubt regarding a predator's attack (derusah) based on a Double Doubt. While some authorities hold it is not a "true" Double Doubt because the first doubt involves a Torah prohibition, everyone agrees that a Double Doubt is effective even with a Presumption of Prohibition, as a living animal is always under a "Presumption of Prohibition" [until properly slaughtered]. Now, if the Rav is challenging a doubt that occurred during the slaughter itself, this is certainly not a valid challenge—as noted in Mishbetzot Zahav—for what does a doubt in slaughter have to do with a doubt regarding a predator's attack? We only say a Double Doubt is ineffective against a Presumption of Prohibition when they are interdependent (i.e., the presumption and the doubts concern the same matter). For instance, regarding a living animal's presumption of prohibition, the presumption concerns the validity of the slaughter, and the doubts also concern the slaughter. But where the doubt is not about the slaughter—such as a doubt of derusah—a Double Doubt is certainly permitted, because regarding derusah, we have no Presumption of Prohibition; on the contrary, every animal is presumed not to have been attacked. This was also written in the book Elya Rabbah (page 50b) in the margin. However, if the Rav's challenge refers to the "Presumption of Prohibition" regarding the wing, he is certainly correct in his challenge, and even the Mishbetzot Zahav would agree. But a Double Doubt regarding the slaughter itself certainly cannot be permitted, as it constitutes a literal Presumption of Prohibition.

text.0_, 140_Siman, 7_Seif, 0_Paragraph: That is, images made specifically to represent the sun and the moon, etc. Since the author did not write "and similarly images made in the shape of the sun, etc." and instead wrote "images made specifically," it implies that only in these specific cases are they forbidden. But a simple round shape resembling the sun, or a plain circular arc resembling the moon, would be permitted since it’s not customary to worship in this manner.  This is also explicitly mentioned by Rambam, who writes: “Images of the sun and moon do not refer to someone finding a circle and saying ‘this is the sun’ or a round arc and saying ‘this is the moon.’ Rather, those who create talismans associate specific shapes with the stars to the extent that they claim ‘the image of the sun is a crowned king seated in a chariot,’ and when they speak of an image of the sun or moon, they mean a form specifically attributed to them.”  This is also the interpretation of Rabbi Ovadiah of Bartenura, and it is evident from Rashi, who interprets “images of the sun and moon” as referring to astrological signs, indicating that he meant these specific forms. This contradicts the Turei Zahav’s (Taz’s) opinion that his teacher, Rabbi Meir Eisenstadt (the Maharam Esh), wrote that it is forbidden to create any images of the sun and moon. The Taz implies that if images made by those who create talismans are forbidden, then certainly a simple round shape representing the sun or moon would also be forbidden. However, this is incorrect, as explained, and the Taz may have misunderstood the basis for the Shulchan Aruch’s words.  The Shulchan Aruch states in section 4 that images of the sun and moon are forbidden, both in raised and engraved forms, both to create them and to keep them. The prohibition applies even to a simple circle, because it appears like a depiction of celestial objects sinking into the heavens, as the commentators mention later. This also aligns with the Talmud’s depiction of Rabban Gamliel, who used various models of the moon for court testimony purposes.  One can argue that certainly, if someone creates or keeps an image of the sun or moon for practical purposes, even in a simple circular form, it is forbidden because the verse “Do not make [idols] for yourselves” prohibits it. Additionally, retaining such images raises suspicions, as one might question why they are kept at all. However, finding such images without any clear association with idol worship is permitted, as there is no concern that they were worshiped. This reasoning is supported by Rabbi Yerucham, who allows enjoyment of these items in cases where idol worship is uncommon, while still forbidding their open display due to possible suspicion. And in section 4, where the Shulchan Aruch forbids images of angels, cherubim, and other celestial beings, the author permits them if they are simply found rather than made. This is supported by the Tur (a major halachic authority) who also writes this. Therefore, images of the sun and moon that are found, without worshipful intent, should not be considered suspect since it is no longer customary to use these images for idolatry. The great sage Rabbi Meir of Lublin left this issue unresolved, questioning Rashi’s interpretation. However, in my humble opinion, the matter is straightforward as I have explained.
text.0_, 140_Siman, 9_Seif, 0_Paragraph: If the objects are esteemed, they are forbidden. C’est exactement l’interprétation de tous les poskim qui n’ont pas rapporté l’avis « הך דרש"י בשם רבו עכ"ל ». (On se demande ainsi comment il leur est venu à l’esprit de rejeter l’opinion de Rachi, et ils ont répondu que cela ne concerne pas ici du tout ce qui relève du domaine du sacré – c’est-à-dire la question de la sainteté, comme pour une instruction ou une matière de Torah – qui, lorsqu’on la formule en langue profane, est interdite, alors que le « nom » établi dans un contexte sacré est véritablement un nom, alors qu’en langue profane il n’en a pas le même statut.) De plus, il est permis d’effacer un nom qui a été rédigé en langue profane, comme par exemple « גאט » en langue ashkénaze ou « בו"ג » en langue polonaise ou russe, etc. Ce dont les poskim n’ont pas retenu l’avis « הך דרש"י » s’explique ainsi : nous trouvons en effet que, pour ce qui est de cette subtilité (משהו של גונא), cela est acceptable. C’est pourquoi j’insiste pour dire qu’il faut, dès le départ, prendre toutes les précautions possibles (לכתחלה יש ליזהר בכל מה דאפשר), comme l’exprime également le Rav, mais là où il n’est pas possible de le faire, il ne l’est tout simplement pas. »

text.0_, 239_Siman, 14_Seif, 0_Paragraph: “L’étude de la Torah…”, etc. — C’est ainsi que nous apprenons de Yaakov : toutes les années durant lesquelles il étudia la Torah dans la maison de Chem et Éver, il ne fut pas puni pour elles, bien qu’il ait, de ce fait, négligé la mitsva d’honorer [ses parents].
text.0_, 245_Siman, 6_Seif, 0_Paragraph: Because she is not commanded yet performs. And greater is one who is commanded and performs than one who is not commanded and performs (So wrote the Tur). [The Tosafot wrote] the reason is because one who is commanded is always concerned to overcome his inclination and to fulfill the commandments of his Creator. That is to say, that regarding one who is commanded, there is thus punishment for transgression, and his inclination overpowers him, and he is always concerned to overcome his inclination. But regarding one who is not commanded, there is no punishment here.
text.0_, 259_Siman, 0_Seif, 0_Paragraph: "Parmi les autres mitsvot positives" – Parce qu’il risque d'etre karet si, en grandissant, il ne se circoncit pas, comme cela est mentionné dans le chapitre suivant.
text.0_, 260_Siman, 0_Seif, 0_Paragraph: "Et on ne circoncit pas, etc." – Et si on a transgressé et que l’on a circoncis sans son consentement, dans un cas où le père est lui-même mohel, il est tenu de lui donner dix pièces d'or, comme cela a été expliqué dans le Ḥoshen Mishpat, à la fin du chapitre 382.
text.0_, 275_Siman, 11_Seif, 0_Paragraph: Il est interdit d’effacer, etc. — Dans une responsa, j’ai longuement traité de ces lois, et j’y ai conclu que : un nom profane, mais écrit comme un des Noms saints, par exemple dans le verset “vous serez comme des dieux” (והייתם כאלהים) et semblables, il est permis de l’effacer. De même, un Nom sacré qui n’a pas été écrit pour la sainteté du Nom, il est permis de l’effacer, mais uniquement pour une correction. En revanche, pour le découper et l’enterrer, c’est permis même si ce n’est pas pour une correction. Mais si le Nom a été écrit pour sa sainteté, même le découper et l’enterrer pour corriger est interdit. Et si de nombreux Noms ont été écrits sans intention (de sainteté) dans un Sefer Torah, il est interdit de les effacer, même si c’est pour une correction, car cela donne l’apparence d’un Sefer Torah tacheté (irrégulier) — voir là-bas.*
text.0_, 288_Siman, 2_Seif, 0_Paragraph: If one places their mezuzah on the inside of the door, retroactively it is valid - this seems to be the opinion of the Tur and of R. Moshe Isserlis, but according to the Nimmukei Yosef and to the Rambam it would be invalid, and this was also the ruling of the Beit Yosef. Therefore, if one did so one should put it up again in the proper place on the outside. However, in the book Maadanei Hamelech (76a) he describes houses open to the public domain where idolators live, and as a result the Jews put up their mezuzot behind their doors. He writes that those who do so have on what to rely upon, namely the words of the Tur and Isserlis.
text.0_, 375_Siman, 13_Seif, 0_Paragraph: "But we are accustomed that they do not pray on Shabbats and holidays" - And similarly are they forbidden to do so on the high holidays; and this is what Rabbi Yaakov ben Moshe Levi Moelin (1365-1427) wrote. However, where there is no one better than him to do so, it is permissible. Such has Rabbi Jacob Ben Judah Weil (1st half of the fifteenth century) written in his laws and ways §47.
